To join two sentences with "care": "Am o colegă. Colega e din Cluj." → "Am o colegă care e din Cluj."
To use "pe care" with the resumptive pronoun: "cartea pe care am citit-o".
To use the relative dative: căruia, căreia, cărora.
To recognise the relative genitive: al cărui, a cărei, ai căror, ale căror.
To use "cine" and "ce" as relative pronouns.
Monday morning, at the office. Ana shows Nora the photos from Friday's party, which Nora couldn't come to. Nora doesn't know all her colleagues yet.
Look, these are the photos from the party. Pity you didn't come!
I was at "Ceasul" with Radu. But tell me who's who. Who is the man holding the cake?
That's Mr Rusu! Didn't you recognise him? He's the man who signs your timesheet every month.
I didn't recognise him at all without a tie! And the woman laughing next to him?
That's Doina, from accounting. She's the colleague you sent the Casa Wolphard invoices to last week.
Ah, that's her! She answered me very nicely. And the young man whose arm she's holding?
That's Matei, her husband. He's a watchmaker. He has a small workshop on Napoca Street.
A watchmaker? Really? Ana, I know a man whose pendulum clock hasn't worked for ten years. He's tried everything.
Mr Grigore? I've heard the story. Everyone in the neighbourhood knows it. But Matei is very good. He's the man everyone takes the old clocks that nobody else can repair any more.
Do you think he'd like to have a look at it?
I'll ask Doina tonight. But be careful: Matei doesn't talk much. He's the kind of man who likes clocks more than people.
Then he'll get on perfectly with Mr Grigore.
a ține: is holding (has in hand)
"nu l-ai recunoscut" = you didn't know who he was (past)
"îl ține de braț" = holds his arm
"a cărui pendulă" = whose pendulum clock (relative genitive)
"genul de om" = the kind of person
"se va înțelege" = will get on well (future)
Stress on the first syllable: CĂ-ru-ia, CĂ-re-ia, CĂ-ro-ra. The final "ia" sounds like "ya".
Said together, without a pause: "pecare". The pause comes after: "cartea pe care… am citit-o".
When the relative clause gives extra information (between commas), make small pauses: "Matei, care e ceasornicar, vorbește puțin."
ceas-or-ni-CAR: stress on the last syllable.
"Care" joins two sentences and replaces a noun. As a subject it doesn't change for gender or number.
I have a colleague. The colleague is from Cluj. → I have a colleague who is from Cluj.
This is the man who repairs clocks.
I see the houses that are on the hill.
In Romanian, "care" is used both for people and for things.
When "care" is the direct object of the verb, it takes "pe". Careful: the verb also keeps the short pronoun (îl, o, îi, le). This is a compulsory rule in Romanian!
The girl you see is Doina.
Without "pe" and without the pronoun ("cartea care am citit") it sounds wrong. It is a very common beginner's mistake.
When the relative clause answers the question "to whom?", use the dative. Here too the verb keeps the short dative pronoun (îi, le).
The short form "cărei" appears mostly in the genitive: "a cărei". As a dative pronoun on its own, use "căreia".
4. The genitive: al cărui, a cărei…
The relative genitive means "whose". The form depends on two things: the owner and the thing owned.
A man whose pendulum clock doesn't work. (the man's clock)
A woman whose son is a musician. (the woman's son)
At A2 level it is enough to recognise these forms. You will use them actively later.
"Cine" means "the person who", and "ce" means "the thing that". They are used without a noun before them.
The early bird catches the worm. (proverb: whoever gets up early goes far)
In everyday speech "ce" sometimes replaces "care": "omul ce stă acolo". It is more literary or more colloquial. You should use "care".

There are people who come to the house with flowers. There are people who come with cakes. And there is Radu, who always comes with something unexpected. On Thursday evening, he came with a notebook.
It was an old blue notebook with dog-eared corners. The cover was stained with oil. Radu put it on the kitchen table, between the teapot and the plate of cozonac that Mrs Pop had made.
"Mum found it yesterday in our attic," he said. "It was in a box that nobody had opened for ten years. The box with Grandpa's things."

Mrs Pop took the notebook in her hands. I saw her fingers trembling. She recognised the handwriting at once: small, slanting letters, written with a pencil that Vasile always sharpened with his pocket knife.
On the first page it said: "The pendulum clock. Instructions for whoever will look after it."

Nora leaned over Mrs Pop's shoulder. I jumped onto the empty chair, from where I could see everything. In the notebook there were drawings: little wheels, springs, a small key, arrows. Next to each drawing there were handwritten explanations.
"Grandpa knew how to repair clocks?" asked Nora.

"He knew nothing," laughed Mrs Pop, her eyes moist. "But he learned. After he inherited the clock, he went every Saturday, for a whole year, to an old watchmaker in the centre. The man he took the clock to was called Mr Iosif. Vasile asked him to teach him the trade. And Mr Iosif, who had no children, taught him everything he knew."
Radu turned the pages slowly. Around the middle of the notebook, he found a page on which was written in big letters: "The secret of the clock".
All three looked at one another. I pricked up my ears.

Mrs Pop read aloud: "This clock has a little wheel that Mr Iosif made with his own hands in 1952, when the old one broke. This wheel is more delicate than the others. Whoever wants the clock to run must know one thing: the wheel is never tightened all the way. You leave a quarter of a turn free. Otherwise, the clock stops."
The kitchen fell silent. Only the fridge could be heard.
"A quarter of a turn," Nora repeated softly. "Mr Grigore tightened everything. He put in new parts. He did everything perfectly. Too perfectly."
"Grandpa didn't have time to tell him," said Radu. "He fell ill too quickly."

Mrs Pop closed the notebook and held it to her chest, like a letter. Then she said something I will never forget: "Vasile always left me little notes. In my coat pocket, in the cookbook, under the pillow. And look, he has left me one more."
Radu wanted to take the notebook to "Ceasul" straight away. But Mrs Pop stopped him. "Not tonight. Tomorrow. And we'll all three take it. No, all four of us." And she looked at me.
I understood then that I am a tomcat who is taken seriously. About time too.
the attic (the space under the roof)
"n-o deschisese" = had not opened it before (pluperfect)
"va avea grijă de" = will look after
"am ciulit urechile" = I listened very carefully
"n-a apucat să" = didn't have time to
